🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

Thomas Aquinas was a friar and teacher who lived in Italy and France about 750 years ago. He was big, quiet and slow to speak, and some students called him "the dumb ox." His teacher, Albert the Great, is said to have answered that one day the whole world would hear this ox bellow. Thomas became one of the most famous thinkers of the Middle Ages.

His great book, the Summa Theologica, is a giant set of questions. Each one is asked like this: "Whether ...?" Then Thomas does something surprising. Before he gives his own answer, he lists the best reasons against it, as fairly as he can. Only then does he answer, and then he replies to every reason he listed.

blocks.name: gb-summa-article
blocks.cap: Press "Next part" to build an article one step at a time: the question, the objections, "On the contrary", "I answer that", and the replies.

blocks.html: His most famous question is "Whether God exists?" Thomas starts from things anyone can see, like a ball that rolls because a foot kicked it, and asks: what started the chain? He gives five ways of answering, which we look at in the full lesson.

🧩 Try this

Write an article like Thomas. Pick a small question, such as "Whether dogs are better pets than cats?" or "Whether bedtime should be later on weekends?" Write: (1) Objections: two good reasons for the side you disagree with. (2) On the contrary: one thing someone wise has said on your side. (3) I answer that: your answer and why. (4) Replies: a fair answer to each objection. Read it to someone. Was it hard to make the other side sound strong?
Thomas believed that faith and reason are friends. Both, he thought, come from God, so the truth found by careful thinking can never really fight the truth taught by faith.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Thomas Aquinas (c. 1225–1274) was born at Roccasecca, near Aquino, south of Rome, into a noble family. As a young man he joined the Dominicans, a new order of preaching friars. His family was so set against it that they kept him at home for about a year, but he held firm. He studied under Albert the Great in Paris and Cologne and taught at the University of Paris and in Italy.

His century was busy with new learning. Most of Aristotle's works had just been translated into Latin, with commentaries by Muslim and Jewish thinkers such as Avicenna, Averroes and Maimonides. Some Christians feared Aristotle; others followed him too far. Aquinas set out to show how the best of this philosophy could fit with Christian faith. He began the Summa Theologica ("summary of theology") around 1265, as a teaching book for beginners, and left it unfinished at his death in 1274.

The Summa has three parts: the First Part on God and creation (this rung), the Second Part on human action, happiness, virtue and law (the next two rungs), and the Third Part on Christ and the sacraments. Each part is divided into questions, and each question into articles.

blocks.name: gb-summa-article
blocks.cap: Build Article 3 of Question 2 step by step, then try the other articles from later rungs.

blocks.html: Every article has the same five parts: the question ("Whether ...?"); objections ("It seems that ..."), the strongest arguments for the view he will reject; "On the contrary" (Latin Sed contra), an authority on the other side; "I answer that" (Latin Respondeo), his own reasoned answer; and replies to the objections. It is the form of a university debate, written down.
Stating your opponents' arguments at full strength before answering is still a good test of an argument. If you cannot answer the best case against you, you have not finished thinking.

The Summa opens by asking whether we need any teaching beyond philosophy (Question 1). Aquinas answers yes. Some truths about God, such as that God exists, can be reached by reason, though only by a few people, after a long time and with many mistakes. Others, such as the Trinity, he holds can be known only because God has revealed them. So both are needed.

In a famous reply in the same question he says that grace does not destroy nature but perfects it. Faith, as he sees it, builds on human reason the way a teacher builds on what a student already knows.

Question 2 asks three things. Is it self-evident that God exists? Aquinas says it is self-evident in itself but not to us, because we do not know what God is; so it needs showing. (Here he answers an argument made famous by Anselm, that God is "that than which nothing greater can be thought," and does not accept it as a proof.) Can it be shown? Yes, he says, from God's effects, the way we reason from smoke to fire. Does God exist? Here come the five ways.

"Motion" for Aquinas means any change from being able to be something to actually being it, as wood that can be hot becomes hot in a fire. Nothing, he argues, brings itself from "can be" to "is"; something already actual must do it. And the chain of movers cannot go on forever, or there would be no first mover, and so no movers after it.

blocks.name: gb-five-ways
blocks.cap: Pick a way, then step back along its chain until you reach Aquinas's key premise and his conclusion.

head: Way
Starts from
Arrives at
rows: A first mover, moved by no other
Things have causes; nothing causes itself
Things come to be and pass away
A being that exists necessarily, of itself
Things are more and less good, true, noble
Something best, the cause of goodness in all
Things without minds act toward ends
An intelligent being who directs them
blocks.cap: The five ways, summarized in our own words.

blocks.title: The shape of the first way
blocks.q: Set out the first way as numbered premises and a conclusion.
steps: 1. Some things are in motion (we see it).
2. Whatever is in motion is moved by something else.
3. The chain of movers cannot go back forever.
4. So there is a first mover, moved by no other (from 1, 2 and 3).
5. This first mover is what people call God (Aquinas's closing step).
blocks.a: Premises 2 and 3 do the work; most later debate is about them, and about the step from 4 to 5.

blocks.html: Thinking the chain in the second way runs back in time, like parents and grandparents. Aquinas means causes acting at once, here and now, as a hand moves a stick that moves a stone. In fact he held (Question 46) that reason alone cannot prove the world had a beginning in time; he believed it did, on faith.

blocks.text: What God is, and is not

blocks.html: After showing that God exists, Aquinas warns that we cannot know what God is in himself, only what he is not. God is not made of parts, not changing, not limited. He calls God simple, perfect, good, infinite, everywhere, unchanging, eternal and one (Questions 3 to 11). When we use words like "good" or "wise" of God, he says (Question 13), we use them neither in exactly the same sense as of people nor in a totally different one, but by analogy: they point to something real in God that far exceeds what the words mean for us.
The first objection in Article 3 is the oldest one: if God were infinitely good, there would be no evil, but there is. Aquinas answers with Augustine.

blocks.text: Creation, angels and the human soul

items: Creation (Questions 44 to 46): God makes all things from nothing, freely, and holds them in being at every moment.
Angels (Questions 50 to 64): pure minds without bodies. Aquinas's careful treatment earned him the title "the Angelic Doctor."

The human soul (Questions 75 to 89): the soul is the "form" of the body, what makes a living human body human. Against Plato, who pictured a soul using a body, Aquinas follows Aristotle: a person is one thing, body and soul together. Yet he argues the soul can survive death, because thinking is not the act of a bodily organ.

blocks.html: Aquinas presents all this as reasoned teaching within his Christian faith. Readers of every belief have studied the Summa for its arguments and its method.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

Read a few articles and you meet the whole library of the Middle Ages: Aristotle, whom Aquinas calls simply "the Philosopher"; Augustine, quoted more than anyone else; Boethius; the writer called Dionysius; the Muslim philosophers Avicenna and Averroes ("the Commentator"); and the Jewish philosopher Maimonides ("Rabbi Moses"). Aquinas disagrees with many of them and still treats each with respect, as a partner in a search for truth.

Aquinas's work was argued over in his own day. Some ideas linked with him were among the propositions condemned by the bishop of Paris in 1277, and Franciscan thinkers such as Duns Scotus offered rival systems. He was declared a saint in 1323. In 1879 Pope Leo XIII urged Catholic schools to study his philosophy, and it is still taught today.

Later philosophers tested the five ways hard. David Hume (Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion, 1779) questioned whether order in nature points to one designer; Immanuel Kant (1781) argued that reasoning from the world to a first cause goes beyond what reason can know. Defenders answer that the five ways are about causes acting here and now, not a story about the past, and that Aquinas's "first" means something quite different from a first item in a series. The debate continues among philosophers today.

items: Can a chain of causes go back forever? Does it matter whether the causes act one after another or all at once?
Is it fair to call the end of each way "God"? What extra steps would you need?
Aquinas says we know more about what God is not than what God is. Can we talk sensibly about something we cannot picture?
Is stating the other side's best arguments a good habit in every disagreement?

blocks.html: Later on this ladder, Dante places Aquinas among the wise in the heaven of the Sun, and Descartes, Hume and Kant take up the same questions in new ways.

💬 Talk about it together

  1. Why do you think Aquinas wrote out the arguments against his own view first? Would that help or hurt in a family argument?
  2. Aquinas thought faith and reason could not truly conflict. What do you think he would do if they seemed to?
  3. Pick one of the five ways. Explain it to someone in your own words, with an everyday example.
  4. Is there anything you believe that you could not prove? Is there anything you could prove that others doubt?
  5. Aquinas was called "the dumb ox" because he was quiet. Have you known someone quiet who turned out to be very wise?

blocks.html: A note for parents: This rung touches on questions of law and conscience. It presents Aquinas's views and those of his main critics, and takes no side.

Choose a path

  • 🌱 For young readers
  • 📖 For teens and adults
  • 🔭 Going deeper

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

What would make you happy forever? A pile of money? Being famous? Being the strongest kid in the world? Thomas Aquinas asked this question about 750 years ago, and he tested the answers one by one, like a detective crossing suspects off a list.

blocks.name: gb-happy-goods
blocks.cap: Tap each card to see why Aquinas crossed it off. Then press "Aquinas's answer."

blocks.html: His test was simple: if you want something only to get something else, it cannot be the last thing you want. Money is for buying things. Fame is what other people think, and they can change their minds. Even good feelings come and go. Aquinas decided that only God could fill the human heart completely.

He also wrote about habits. If you practice the piano every day, playing gets easier, until one day it feels natural. Aquinas said being good works the same way. Telling the truth, sharing and being brave become easier each time, until they are part of you. A good habit like that is called a virtue.

🧩 Try this

The "what for?" game. Write down five things you want. For each one, ask "What do I want it for?" and write the answer. Then ask again about that answer. (Shoes: to play soccer. Soccer: because it's fun with friends. Friends: ...) Where does each chain stop? Do any stop in the same place?

Aquinas wrote about rules and laws too. A good law, he said, has to make sense, has to help everyone and not just the person who made it, and has to be told to people so they know it. Can you think of a family rule that passes all three tests?

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

blocks.text: The Second Part: how to live

blocks.html: The First Part of the Summa was about God and creation. The Second Part, the largest, is about human beings as free agents: what we aim at, how we act, and what helps or harms us on the way. Aquinas divides it in two. The First Part of the Second Part (in Latin, Prima Secundae) gives the general principles: happiness, human acts, feelings, habits, virtues, sin, law and grace. This rung covers it. The next rung turns to particular virtues.

Aquinas begins where Aristotle's Ethics begins. Everything we do, we do for some end, and the ends form chains: I study to pass, pass to graduate, graduate to work. The chain cannot go on forever, so there is a last end, wanted for itself. Everyone agrees, he says, that this last end is happiness. The hard part is saying what happiness is.

blocks.name: gb-happy-goods
blocks.cap: The eight candidates of Question 2, with Aquinas's reason for rejecting each (in our own words).

blocks.html: One by one he rules out wealth, honor, fame, power, health and beauty, pleasure, and even the goods of the soul such as knowledge. His reason in the last article is the deepest: the human will reaches for goodness without limit, so no limited good can bring it to rest.

Perfect happiness, he concludes (Question 3), is seeing God as he is, which he believes belongs to the life to come. But he does not dismiss this life. There is a real, imperfect happiness here, found above all in knowing the truth and in living virtuously, helped by friends and by enough of the goods of the body.

items: Human acts (Questions 6 to 21): an act is fully human when it comes from reason and will. Whether it is good depends on what is done, why, and in what circumstances.

Passions, or feelings (Questions 22 to 48): Aquinas lists eleven. Six concern good and evil simply: love and hatred, desire and aversion, joy and sorrow. Five concern good or evil that is hard to reach or avoid: hope and despair, fear and daring, and anger. Feelings are not bad in themselves; they become good or bad by how reason guides them.
Habits (Questions 49 to 54): a habit is a settled way of being, built up by repeated acts, that makes action easy and sure.

blocks.html: A virtue is a good habit (Question 55). Aquinas sorts them: intellectual virtues perfect the mind (wisdom, understanding, knowledge, art, and prudence); moral virtues perfect our choices and feelings; and the theological virtues, faith, hope and charity, direct us to God and are, he holds, given by God. Four moral virtues are "cardinal," or hinge, virtues: prudence, justice, fortitude (courage) and temperance.
Following Aristotle, he says a moral virtue lies in a mean between two extremes, set by reason (Question 64). Courage lies between cowardice and recklessness.

blocks.title: Finding the mean
blocks.q: Aquinas, like Aristotle, puts each moral virtue between a "too little" and a "too much." Name the extremes around generosity with money.
steps: Ask what the virtue is about: giving and spending money.
Too little giving: stinginess. Too much: wastefulness.
The mean is not a fixed amount; it is what reason judges right for this person, here and now.
blocks.a: Stinginess and wastefulness; generosity is the mean between them.

blocks.html: Near the end of the First Part of the Second Part come the questions on law (Questions 90 to 108), still among the most read pages of the Summa. Aquinas first asks what a law is. Four articles give four parts of an answer.

A law, for Aquinas, has four marks: it is a rule of reason, not mere will; it aims at the common good, not one person's advantage; it is made by the one who has care of the community; and it is made public ("promulgated"), since a rule nobody knows cannot guide anyone.

blocks.name: gb-law-kinds
blocks.cap: Tap each kind of law. Eternal law contains the natural law, from which human laws are worked out; divine law, given in Scripture, stands alongside.

blocks.html: The natural law (Question 94) begins from a first rule that every practical mind knows: good is to be done and pursued, and evil avoided. From our natural inclinations come further rules: to preserve our life, to raise and teach our children, to know the truth about God, and to live in society with others.

Human law (Questions 95 to 97) is worked out from the natural law in two ways. Some laws follow as conclusions ("do not murder" follows from "do no harm"). Others settle details that reason leaves open, such as a particular penalty, or which side of the road to drive on. Human law, he adds, should not try to forbid every vice, only the graver ones that harm others and that most people can avoid; and it may change as people and times change.

Thinking Aquinas held that any command from a ruler is a law. He argues that a human rule that goes against the natural law is not truly a law but a corruption of law, and that unjust laws do not bind in conscience, though one may still obey them to avoid scandal or disorder. This idea had a long history: Martin Luther King Jr. quoted Augustine and Aquinas on unjust laws in his Letter from Birmingham Jail (1963). Legal philosophers who separate law from morality, such as John Austin and H. L. A. Hart, reject this view; the debate between the two schools goes on.
The Part ends with grace (Questions 109 to 114): the help Aquinas believes God gives so that people can reach an end beyond their natural powers.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

Much of this Part is a conversation with Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics, which Aquinas also wrote a commentary on. Both say happiness is the last end, that virtue is a habit and a mean, and that we become good by doing good acts. Aquinas adds what Aristotle did not have: a last end beyond this life, the theological virtues, and the eternal law. Readers still argue over whether he completes Aristotle or changes him.

Aquinas's questions on law became the classic statement of natural law theory. Later thinkers on this ladder, such as John Locke and the writers of the American founding, used natural law and natural rights in their own ways. Critics such as Jeremy Bentham called natural rights "nonsense upon stilts," and the legal positivists hold that what the law is and what it ought to be are separate questions.

items: Is there a last end that all people aim at, or does each person choose their own?
Can a law be unjust and still be a law? What would follow either way?
Should the law try to make people good, or only keep them from harming one another? Aquinas gives a middle answer. Do you agree?
Is a virtue really like a habit, or does goodness need to be chosen fresh each time?

blocks.html: On this ladder, compare Aristotle's Ethics and Politics, then Hobbes, Locke and Rousseau on law and the common good.

💬 Talk about it together

  1. Make a list of things people think will make them happy. Which would Aquinas cross off, and why?
  2. What is a habit you have worked to build? Did it get easier with practice?
  3. Think of a rule at home or school. Does it pass Aquinas's four tests: reasonable, for everyone's good, made by the right person, and made known?
  4. Courage lies between cowardice and recklessness. Can you name a time when someone was too cautious, or not cautious enough?
  5. Why might a law not try to forbid every wrong thing?

blocks.html: A note for parents: This rung presents Thomas Aquinas's Christian teaching on faith, hope, charity and the sacraments as his own views, without arguing for or against them. It mentions his questions on war without detail.

Choose a path

  • 🌱 For young readers
  • 📖 For teens and adults
  • 🔭 Going deeper

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

In the last parts of his great book, Thomas Aquinas wrote about seven virtues, seven strong good habits. Four of them help anyone live well: prudence (good sense), justice (fairness), fortitude (courage) and temperance (self-control). Three more he called the virtues that lead to God: faith, hope and charity, which means love.

blocks.name: gb-virtue-wheel
blocks.cap: Tap each virtue on the wheel. The inner ring holds faith, hope and charity; the outer ring holds the four "hinge" virtues.

blocks.html: Thomas said that charity is a kind of friendship with God. And just as you are kind to your best friend's little brother because you love your friend, charity is kind to everyone, even people who are hard to like.

Thomas worked on his book for years, writing and dictating to helpers. Near the end of his life he stopped writing, and the book was never finished. His friends finished the last pages using things he had written earlier.

🧩 Try this

A virtue week. Draw a circle and divide it into seven slices, one for each virtue. Each day, look for one example of a virtue, in a story you read, at home or at school, and write or draw it in its slice. Which slice filled up fastest? Which was hardest to spot?

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Volume 18 of the set carries the Summa on from where the last rung stopped. The Second Part of the Second Part (in Latin, Secunda Secundae) takes the virtues one at a time: first the three theological virtues, faith, hope and charity, and then the four cardinal virtues, each with the vices opposed to it. The Third Part is about Christ and the sacraments. Aquinas stopped writing in December 1273, partway through the sacrament of penance; after his death his followers completed the work with a Supplement drawn from his earlier writings. This rung follows the selections in the set, which center on faith, hope and charity.

blocks.name: gb-virtue-wheel
blocks.cap: Seven virtues of the Second Part of the Second Part, with the questions that treat each and the vices set against them.

blocks.html: Aquinas defines faith with the Letter to the Hebrews: "the substance of things to be hoped for, the evidence of things that appear not." Its object, he says, is God as the first truth. To believe is an act of the mind, which assents to what God has revealed, moved by the will. That is why faith differs from knowledge: what we see proved, we know; what we accept on another's word, we believe. He holds that the same thing cannot be both known and believed by the same person in the same respect.

Hope, for Aquinas, looks forward to a good that is future, hard to reach, but possible: eternal happiness with God, reached with God's help. It has two opposites. Despair gives up on that good; presumption takes it for granted. Like a moral virtue, hope steers between them.

Question 23 asks whether charity is friendship. Aquinas borrows Aristotle's account of friendship: a love that wishes the friend well, is returned, and rests on something the friends share. God, he holds, shares his own happiness with people.

blocks.title: Why charity is the greatest
blocks.q: Aquinas, with Paul's "the greatest of these is charity" (1 Corinthians 13:13), argues that charity is the highest virtue (Question 23, Article 6). Lay out his reasoning.
steps: The theological virtues are higher than the others, because they reach God himself.
Faith reaches God as a source of truth we do not yet see; hope reaches God as a good we do not yet have.
Charity reaches God as he is, resting in him, not in something still to come.
So charity is the greatest, and it directs all the other virtues to their last end, which is why he calls it their "form."
blocks.a: Charity, because it rests in God himself and gives every other virtue its direction.

blocks.html: The questions on charity are full of everyday matters. Charity loves God first, then oneself, then one's neighbor; it loves enemies too, in the sense of wishing them good and being ready to help. Its fruits are joy, peace, mercy, kindness and giving to those in need. Opposed to it are hatred, envy, discord and quarreling. In this same section Aquinas asks whether it is always wrong to wage war (Question 40), and gives the conditions that became the classic statement of "just war" teaching: the right authority, a just cause and a right intention. Writers on war and peace have debated these conditions ever since.

items: Prudence (Questions 47 to 56): practical wisdom, right reason about what to do.
Justice (Questions 57 to 122): giving each person what is due to them. Here Aquinas treats fair prices, honest lending, telling the truth, gratitude and religion as a part of justice.
Fortitude (Questions 123 to 140): firmness in danger, with patience and perseverance.
Temperance (Questions 141 to 170): keeping our desires within the measure that reason sets.

blocks.html: The Third Part asks why God became man and how, then turns to the sacraments, which Aquinas describes as signs that, as he believes, also bring about the grace they signify. He counts seven, matching them to the stages of a person's life, from birth (baptism) to illness and death. He presents all of this as the teaching of his faith, argued with the same objections and replies as the rest.

Picturing the Summa as a book of rules. It is a book of arguments. Even on faith and charity, Aquinas lists objections and answers them with reasons, and he often finds some truth in the view he rejects.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

On or near the feast of Saint Nicholas in December 1273, Aquinas stopped writing. His companion, Reginald of Piperno, later reported that when urged to go on, Thomas said that all he had written seemed like straw compared with what he had seen. The story comes from the testimony gathered for his canonization, and readers have taken it in many ways. He died on 7 March 1274 at the abbey of Fossanova, on his way to a church council in Lyon.

Aquinas also wrote poetry: he is traditionally credited with the Latin hymns for the feast of Corpus Christi, such as Pange lingua, still sung today. His account of the virtues shaped Dante's Divine Comedy, where Saints Peter, James and John examine Dante on faith, hope and charity, and it remains a reference point in moral philosophy, including the recent revival of "virtue ethics."

items: Aquinas says the same thing cannot be both known and believed by the same person. Do you agree? Can you believe something and also have good evidence for it?
Is hope a virtue, or only a feeling? Can it be practiced?
What does it mean to love an enemy? Is it the same as liking them?
Can a war ever be just? What would have to be true?

blocks.html: Compare Aristotle on friendship in the Ethics, Augustine's City of God on the two loves, and later, Spinoza and Kant on what morality asks of us.

💬 Talk about it together

  1. Which of the seven virtues do you think is hardest? Which is easiest for you?
  2. Aquinas says despair and presumption are both opposed to hope. Can you think of an example of each?
  3. What makes a friendship? Use Aquinas's three marks: wishing each other well, love returned, something shared.
  4. Why do you think Aquinas stopped writing before the book was done? What would you do with an unfinished project you loved?
  5. Is it possible to be kind to someone you don't like? How?

blocks.html: A note for parents: The Inferno describes the punishments of Hell vividly. This lesson summarizes them gently and quotes none of them. Young readers can follow Cantos I to IV and the end of Canto XXXIV, or a retelling.

Choose a path

  • 🌱 For young readers
  • 📖 For teens and adults
  • 🔭 Going deeper

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

Dante Alighieri was a poet in the city of Florence, in Italy, about 700 years ago. He wrote a giant poem about an imaginary journey through the three realms where, as Christians of his time believed, souls go after death: Hell, Purgatory and Heaven. The first part, the Inferno, is the journey through Hell.

The poem begins with Dante lost in a dark forest at night. He tries to climb a sunny hill, but three wild animals block his path: a spotted leopard, a lion and a hungry wolf. Just when he is ready to give up, a figure appears. It is the spirit of Virgil, a Roman poet Dante loved, who has come to guide him. The only way out, Virgil says, is the long way: down through the whole of Hell, and up the other side.

blocks.name: gb-dante-cosmos
blocks.cap: Hell is shaped like a giant funnel with nine circles, each smaller than the one above. Step down through them with the buttons, or tap a circle.

blocks.html: Each circle is for a different kind of wrong, and the worst wrongs are at the bottom. Things in Hell happen in ways that fit the wrong: people who let their feelings blow them about are blown by a never-ending wind. At the very bottom is a lake of ice, and in the middle of it, stuck fast, is Satan. Dante and Virgil climb right past him, and at last they come out on the other side of the world, under the stars.
For parents: the Inferno has frightening scenes. Young readers can enjoy Cantos I to IV (the dark wood, the gate and Limbo), and the climb out at the end of Canto XXXIV, or a good retelling.

🧩 Try this

A rhyme chain. Dante wrote in three-line groups where the middle line's rhyme starts the next group: A B A, B C B, C D C. Try it: "The night was long, the forest deep, / I saw no path, I saw no light, / until a voice called through my sleep." Now the next group must rhyme with light in lines 1 and 3. Can you write two more?

blocks.name: gb-terza-rima
blocks.cap: Add tercets and watch the rhymes chain together.

blocks.html:
📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Dante Alighieri (1265–1321) was born in Florence. As a boy he met Beatrice Portinari, who became, in his writing, the great love and guide of his life; she died young in 1290, and he wrote of her in La Vita Nuova ("The New Life"). He served Florence in its fierce political quarrels, and in 1302, while he was away, the winning party sentenced him to exile. He never returned. He wrote the Comedy in exile, finishing it shortly before his death in Ravenna.

He called it simply the Comedy, because it begins in sorrow and ends in joy, and because it is written in the everyday language of Tuscany rather than in Latin. Later readers added "Divine." It has three parts, or canticles, Inferno, Purgatorio and Paradiso, of 34, 33 and 33 cantos: 100 in all. The journey takes place at Easter in the year 1300, when Dante was 35, "midway" through the Bible's span of seventy years.

Dante wrote in terza rima, a rhyme pattern he invented: three-line stanzas rhyming ABA BCB CDC, each one linked to the next. A canto ends with a single line that closes the last rhyme. In Italian the first three lines end vita, oscura, smarrita.

blocks.name: gb-terza-rima
blocks.cap: Count the lines: n tercets plus one closing line make 3n + 1.

blocks.title: Counting lines
blocks.q: A canto has 46 tercets, plus its closing line. How many lines is that?
steps: Each tercet has 3 lines: $46 \times 3 = 138$.
Add the closing line: $138 + 1 = 139$.
blocks.a: 139 lines (Inferno, Canto I, has 136; cantos range from about 115 to 160)

blocks.html: Virgil explains that he was sent by Beatrice, from Heaven, to rescue Dante. Dante chose Virgil because Virgil's Aeneid had already taken a hero into the underworld, and because Virgil was his master in poetry. In the poem Virgil stands for the best that human reason can do, guiding Dante as far as reason can go.

blocks.name: gb-dante-cosmos
blocks.cap: The nine circles from the gate to the center of the Earth, with our own short summaries.

blocks.html: In Canto XI Virgil explains the plan, using Aristotle's Ethics. The upper circles (2 to 5) hold sins of incontinence, failing to control one's desires. Below the walls of the city of Dis lie the sins of malice, done on purpose: first violence (circle 7), then fraud, which is worse because it misuses reason, the gift that makes us human (circles 8 and 9). Treachery against those who trusted you is the very worst.

Each punishment fits its sin, an idea later readers call the contrapasso ("counter-suffering"), from a word one of Dante's characters uses in Canto XXVIII. Those who let desire sweep them along are swept by wind; the angry fight in mud; the cold-hearted traitors are held in ice. The punishments show what the sin was already like.

Dante feels pity for many of the souls he meets. In Canto V, two lovers tell their sad story and he faints from sorrow. Later he grows harder, and Virgil approves. Readers still argue whether the poem wants us to share his pity or to learn to see as divine justice sees.

In the eighth circle, among false advisers, Dante meets the Greek hero Ulysses (Odysseus) wrapped in a flame. Ulysses tells a story found in no ancient book: in old age he sailed his crew west past the edge of the known world, urging them on with a famous speech.

They sail for five months and see a great mountain rising from the sea, and then a storm sinks them. Ulysses' thirst for knowledge is noble; he is in Hell for the tricks of his war, such as the wooden horse of Troy. Readers take the mountain to be Purgatory, the subject of the next canticle.

At the center of the Earth, in the frozen lake, Satan is stuck in ice, and the beating of his huge wings is what freezes it. Virgil carries Dante down Satan's side; past the center, "down" becomes "up," and the two climb a long passage to the far side of the Earth. The canticle ends as they come out to see the stars. All three canticles end with the same word: stelle, "stars."

Reading the Inferno as a list of horrors. Dante's Hell is a moral map: each circle asks what a wrong does to the person who chooses it. And it is only one third of the journey; the poem's aim is the climb that follows.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

Medieval readers looked for several senses in a text: the literal story, and beneath it allegorical, moral and spiritual meanings. The Comedy invites this. Literally, it is one man's journey; allegorically, it is every soul's journey from confusion to clarity. A letter to Dante's patron, Cangrande della Scala, explains the poem this way; scholars still debate whether Dante wrote it.

Dante fills his Hell with people his readers knew: politicians, churchmen, even popes, along with figures from myth and history. His harsh judgments of his own city were part of the poem's power and its risk. He presents these as his judgments within the poem; later readers have often disagreed with them.

About fifty years after Dante's death, Florence paid Boccaccio to lecture on the poem in public, and a 1555 edition first printed the title La Divina Commedia. In English, Henry Francis Cary's blank-verse version (1814) made Dante widely read; Longfellow's line-by-line translation (1867) and Charles Eliot Norton's prose (1891) followed. Painters, composers and poets have returned to it ever since.

items: Is it right for a poet to place real people in Hell? What does Dante risk by doing it?
Is fraud worse than violence, as Dante says? Why might misusing reason be the worst wrong?
Why does Dante pity some sinners, and why does Virgil scold him for it?
What does Ulysses get right, and what does he get wrong?

blocks.html: Dante built on Virgil's Aeneid (Book VI) and on Aquinas's and Aristotle's accounts of virtue and vice, all earlier on this ladder. Milton's Paradise Lost, later on, offers another great poem of Hell and its fallen angel.

💬 Talk about it together

  1. If you were lost in a dark wood, who would you want for a guide, and why?
  2. Dante says each punishment fits its wrong. Is a punishment that "fits" fairer than one that does not?
  3. Dante felt sorry for some of the people he met. Is it good to feel sorry for someone who did wrong?
  4. Ulysses says we were made "virtue to pursue and knowledge high." What do you most want to learn?
  5. Why do you think all three parts of the poem end with the word "stars"?

blocks.html: A note for parents: This rung presents the medieval Christian idea of Purgatory as Dante imagined it, noting that Christians have disagreed about it. Nothing in it needs special care for young readers.

Choose a path

  • 🌱 For young readers
  • 📖 For teens and adults
  • 🔭 Going deeper

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

After their long climb out of Hell, Dante and his guide Virgil come out on a beach at dawn. The stars are bright, the air is fresh, and in front of them rises an enormous mountain from the sea. This is Purgatory, the second part of Dante's great poem, the Purgatorio.

In Dante's poem, Purgatory is a place of hope. The souls here are sorry for the wrongs they did, and they climb the mountain to become good all the way through. On each of seven ledges, called terraces, they practice the opposite of one bad habit. The proud learn to be humble; the grumpy learn to be gentle. And they help each other, singing and praying as they go.

blocks.name: gb-dante-cosmos
blocks.cap: Climb the mountain from the shore to the garden at the top. Tap a level to read about it.

blocks.html: At the gate, an angel marks seven letters on Dante's forehead. On every terrace, an angel brushes one away, and Dante feels lighter, so climbing gets easier the higher he goes. At the very top is a beautiful garden, and there Dante meets Beatrice, the friend he loved, who will guide him the rest of the way.

🧩 Try this

Seven steps up. Draw a mountain with seven ledges. On each ledge, write one bad habit and its opposite good habit: pride and humility, envy and kindness, anger and gentleness, laziness and eagerness, greed and generosity, overeating and moderation, selfish wanting and self-control. Which good habit would you most like to practice this week? Draw yourself on that ledge.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Dante pictures Purgatory as a mountain on an island in the southern ocean, exactly opposite Jerusalem on the globe. (Ulysses glimpsed it before his ship went down.) It was formed, the poem explains, when Satan fell from heaven and the land fled from him. Dante and Virgil arrive at dawn on Easter Sunday, and the poem's mood changes at once.

Unlike Hell, Purgatory has time, sunlight, music and friendship. The souls want to be here; they know their climb will end in Heaven. Prayers of the living, they say, can speed them on. This rests on the teaching of the medieval Church, which Dante shared; later, Protestant reformers rejected the idea of Purgatory. The poem presents it as Dante's faith imagined it.

blocks.name: gb-dante-cosmos
blocks.cap: From the shore to the Earthly Paradise: Ante-Purgatory, the gate, the seven terraces and the garden.

blocks.text: From the shore to the gate

items: The shore (Cantos I and II): the old Roman Cato guards it. Virgil washes Dante's face of the grime of Hell and ties a reed, a plant that bends without breaking, around his waist as a sign of humility. An angel steers a boat of souls across the sea, and among them is Dante's friend Casella, a musician, who sings one of Dante's own poems.
Ante-Purgatory (Cantos III to VIII): souls who put off turning to God must wait before they can begin. Dante meets old friends and talks with rulers resting in a flowered valley.
The gate (Canto IX): three steps, an angel with a sword and two keys, and seven P's, for the Latin peccatum ("sin"), traced on Dante's forehead.

blocks.html: On each terrace the souls are cured of one of the seven capital sins, the roots of the others in medieval teaching. They meditate on examples of the opposite virtue, often from the life of Mary, and on warnings of the vice; an angel sings one of the Beatitudes and brushes away a P. Midway up, Virgil explains why there are seven, in one of the poem's great speeches.

Virgil's point: every act comes from some love. Good acts come from love rightly aimed; wrongs come from love gone astray in one of three ways. Love can be aimed at harm to others (pride, envy and anger); it can be too weak for the highest good (sloth); or it can be too strong for lesser goods (greed, gluttony, and an excessive love of bodily pleasure, called lust).

head: Terrace
Sin
How love went wrong
What the souls do
rows: Sit in plain cloaks, eyes closed
Lie face down on the ground
Walk through a wall of flame
blocks.cap: Our summary of Cantos X to XXVII.

blocks.html: In Canto XVI, on the terrace of anger, a soul explains that the stars may stir our feelings but do not decide our choices: we have free will, and if the world goes wrong, the cause lies in us. On the terrace of greed the mountain shakes and the souls sing, because one of them, the Roman poet Statius, has finished his cleansing. He climbs on with Dante and Virgil to the top.

Before the last climb, Dante must pass through fire. He is terrified until Virgil reminds him that Beatrice waits beyond it. Then, at the top, Virgil gives his last words: Dante's will is now free, upright and whole, and he may follow it; Virgil crowns him master of himself. In the Earthly Paradise, the Garden of Eden, a great procession appears, and Beatrice comes, veiled. When Dante turns to Virgil, Virgil is gone; reason has brought him as far as it can.
Dante drinks from two rivers: Lethe, which takes away the memory of sin, and Eunoë, which restores the memory of good. The canticle ends with him made new and ready to rise to the stars.
Thinking Purgatory is a milder Hell. In the poem they are opposites. Hell's souls are fixed in what they chose; Purgatory's souls are changing, gladly, and every one of them will reach Heaven.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

blocks.text: A poem of friendship and art

blocks.html: Purgatorio is full of artists. Dante meets musicians, painters and poets: the miniaturist Oderisi, who warns that fame passes quickly; Sordello, a poet of Virgil's own Mantua; Statius; and on the last terrace two poets Dante admired, one of whom answers him in Provençal. It is the canticle where Dante thinks hardest about his own art and its pride.

Virgil cannot enter Heaven; in the poem he lives in Limbo, among the good who lived before Christ. His leaving is one of the most moving moments in the poem, and readers still discuss what it means that the guide Dante loved most must turn back.

items: Is Virgil right that every wrong act comes from love gone astray? Try it on an example.
Can people really change their habits from the inside? What helps?
Why does climbing get easier as Dante goes higher?
What does it mean to be "master of yourself"?

blocks.html: Compare Aquinas on the virtues and the passions, two rungs back, and Augustine's City of God, which defines virtue as love set in the right order.

💬 Talk about it together

  1. Which of the seven bad habits do you see most in the world around you? Which good habit would cure it?
  2. In Purgatory the souls help each other. How does helping others make it easier to change?
  3. Why does Dante put Purgatory in the open air, with sunlight and music, instead of underground?
  4. Virgil says every good act and every wrong act comes from some kind of love. Can you think of an example?
  5. How do you think Dante felt when Virgil disappeared? Have you ever had to say goodbye to a guide or teacher?

blocks.html: A note for parents: This rung presents Dante's Christian vision of heaven as his own, without arguing for or against it.

Choose a path

  • 🌱 For young readers
  • 📖 For teens and adults
  • 🔭 Going deeper

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

In the last part of his poem, the Paradiso, Dante flies up into the sky with Beatrice. He does not need a rocket. He looks at Beatrice, Beatrice looks up at the light of heaven, and they rise, faster than lightning, from one sphere to the next.

In Dante's time people pictured the sky as a set of giant, clear spheres nested one inside another, with the Earth at the center. Each sphere carried a shining body: the Moon, then Mercury, Venus, the Sun, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn, then all the fixed stars. Beyond those spun one more sphere that turned all the rest, and beyond everything was the home of God, full of light.

blocks.name: gb-dante-cosmos
blocks.cap: Climb through the heavens from the Moon to the Empyrean. Tap a sphere to read who Dante meets there.

blocks.html: In each heaven Dante meets happy souls who shine like lights. In the heaven of the Sun he meets wise teachers, including Thomas Aquinas, dancing in rings of light. Everything gets brighter as he goes, and Beatrice's smile gets so bright he can hardly look at it. At the very end Dante sees God, and the poem stops, because, he says, there are no words for what he saw.

🧩 Try this

Make the spheres. Cut ten circles of paper, each a little bigger than the last, or stack ten bowls inside one another. Put a small ball or bead in the middle for the Earth. Label each circle: Moon, Mercury, Venus, Sun, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Fixed stars, Primum Mobile, Empyrean. How is this picture different from what we know about the solar system today?

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Paradiso, the last 33 cantos of the Comedy, follows Dante and Beatrice from the top of Mount Purgatory through the heavens to God. It is the hardest canticle to read and, for many readers, the most beautiful. Where Hell was a funnel of darkness, Paradise is made of light, music and motion.

Dante's cosmos is the one taught from Aristotle and Ptolemy: a round Earth at the center, surrounded by turning spheres. The Moon and the Sun counted as "planets," wanderers among the stars, so there were seven planetary spheres, then the sphere of the fixed stars, then the Primum Mobile ("first moved"), which turns all the others. Beyond them, outside space and time, is the Empyrean, God's heaven.

blocks.name: gb-dante-cosmos
blocks.cap: The ten heavens of the Paradiso, with our own summaries of what happens in each.

blocks.title: Counting the heavens
blocks.q: How many moving spheres are there in Dante's heavens, and how many heavens in all?
steps: Seven planets (Moon, Mercury, Venus, Sun, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn): 7 spheres.
Add the fixed stars and the Primum Mobile: $7 + 2 = 9$ moving spheres.
Add the Empyrean, which does not move: $9 + 1 = 10$.
blocks.a: Nine moving spheres, ten heavens in all. Nine, three times three, mattered to Dante, as it did in his early book about Beatrice.

blocks.html: In Canto II Beatrice explains the dark marks on the Moon, and she proposes an experiment: set up three mirrors at different distances, put a light behind you, and see that the far mirror shines as brightly as the near ones, only smaller. It is one of the first descriptions of an experiment in a great poem, though her explanation of the marks is not ours.

blocks.text: Why the blessed appear in different heavens

blocks.html: In the Moon, Dante meets Piccarda, a woman who could not keep her vows. He asks if she wishes for a higher place. She answers that the blessed want only what God wills.

Beatrice then explains (Canto IV) that all the blessed really live together in the Empyrean. They appear in the lower spheres only to show Dante, in a way a human mind can grasp, that they share in heaven's joy in different degrees, and each is content.

items: The Sun (Cantos X to XIV): twelve wise souls form a ring of light around Dante and Beatrice, then a second ring. Thomas Aquinas, a Dominican, tells the life of Saint Francis, and the Franciscan Bonaventure tells the life of Saint Dominic. Each praises the other's founder.
Mars (Cantos XIV to XVIII): Dante's ancestor Cacciaguida tells him he will be exiled, will learn how bitter another man's bread tastes, and must still write everything he has seen.
Jupiter (Cantos XVIII to XX): the souls of just rulers form the shape of an eagle, which speaks with one voice about divine justice.
The fixed stars (Cantos XXII to XXVII): Dante looks down and sees the Earth, so small it makes him smile. Saint Peter examines him on faith, Saint James on hope and Saint John on love.
The Primum Mobile (Cantos XXVII to XXIX): God appears as a single point of intense light, circled by nine rings of angels.
The Empyrean (Cantos XXX to XXXIII): the blessed sit in a vast white rose. Beatrice takes her place in it, and Saint Bernard becomes Dante's last guide.

blocks.html: Bernard prays to Mary for Dante, and Dante is allowed to look into the light of God. He sees three circles of one light, and within them a human likeness, and he struggles to understand how they fit, until a flash of understanding comes. His power to imagine fails, but his will and desire now turn in harmony with God.

Thinking Dante believed heaven is "up in the sky" like a place you could reach by flying. The poem says itself that the spheres are shown to Dante as a picture for the human mind. The Empyrean is beyond space altogether.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

blocks.text: Light and the limits of language

blocks.html: Again and again in the Paradiso Dante says that memory and words fail him. That is not a weakness of the poem but its subject: how can anyone describe what is greater than the mind? Dante answers with images of light, music, circles and a rose, and with Beatrice's growing beauty, which he can describe only by saying he cannot.

Dante's heavens are a medieval picture that later science replaced. Copernicus, Kepler and Galileo, later on this ladder, put the Sun at the center and showed that the heavens are made of the same kind of stuff as the Earth. Galileo himself, as a young man, gave lectures in Florence on the shape and size of Dante's Inferno. The poem's picture of the cosmos is gone, but readers still find in it a vision of an ordered, meaningful universe.

items: Piccarda is content with a lower place. Is it possible to be completely happy without having the most?
Why does Dante need a different guide for each part of the journey: Virgil, then Beatrice, then Bernard?
If words fail, why write at all? What else can a poet do?
Dante saw the Earth from the stars and smiled at how small it was. How might seeing your life "from above" change it?

blocks.html: Compare Ptolemy's Almagest and Aristotle's On the Heavens for Dante's cosmos, Aquinas for his theology, and Milton for another poem of heaven.

💬 Talk about it together

  1. Dante rises by looking at Beatrice, who looks at God. Who helps you "rise" when you are learning something?
  2. Piccarda says "in his will is our tranquillity." What do you think she means?
  3. What is the most beautiful light you have ever seen? Could you describe it to someone who wasn't there?
  4. Dante ends with "the Love ... that moves the sun ... and all the stars." Why might he end a long poem with love?
  5. How is Dante's picture of the sky different from ours? What would he find most surprising about what we know now?

blocks.html: A note for parents: A story of grown-up romance. The lesson keeps to the plot and the ideas about Fortune, faithfulness and language, and quotes only the opening stanza and Chaucer's lines on how language changes.

Choose a path

  • 🌱 For young readers
  • 📖 For teens and adults
  • 🔭 Going deeper

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

Geoffrey Chaucer lived in London about 650 years ago and is often called the father of English poetry. He wrote in the English of his day, called Middle English. It looks strange to us, but if you read it out loud, you can understand more than you expect.

Troilus and Criseyde is a long poem set during the war at Troy, the same war Homer wrote about. Troilus is a young prince of Troy. He loves Criseyde, and with the help of his friend Pandarus they promise to be true to each other. But then Criseyde is sent away to the Greek camp, and she does not keep her promise to come back. It is a sad story about trust, friendship and change.

People in Chaucer's time liked to picture life as a great wheel turned by a lady called Fortune. Sometimes you ride up to the top; then the wheel turns and down you go. Troilus rides the wheel all the way up and all the way down.

blocks.name: gb-fortune-wheel
blocks.cap: Move the slider through the five books of the poem and watch where Troilus is on Fortune's wheel.

blocks.html:
🧩 Try this

Decode Middle English. Read these lines out loud, slowly: "The double sorwe of Troilus to tellen, / That was the king Priamus sone of Troye." Sorwe sounds like sorrow; sone like son. What do the lines mean? (The double sorrow of Troilus to tell, who was King Priam's son, of Troy.) Now try: "Fro wo to wele, and after out of Ioye." The letter I here stands for J.
For parents: this is a grown-up love story. The lesson keeps to the plot and the big ideas, Fortune and faithfulness; the poem's love scenes are better for older readers.

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Geoffrey Chaucer (c. 1343–1400) was the son of a London wine merchant. He served kings as a page, soldier, diplomat and customs official, and traveled to Italy on royal business in the 1370s, where he came to know the works of Dante, Petrarch and Boccaccio. He wrote Troilus and Criseyde in the 1380s, before the Canterbury Tales. It is his longest finished poem, about 8,200 lines in five books.

The story is not in Homer. It grew up in the Middle Ages, in a French poem of the 1100s about Troy, and was retold by Boccaccio in Italian as Il Filostrato. Chaucer used Boccaccio closely but made the story deeper and slower, and gave much more life to Criseyde and to Pandarus. He pretends, playfully, to be translating an old writer he calls "Lollius," who did not exist.

Chaucer wrote the poem in seven-line stanzas rhyming ABABBCC, with ten-syllable lines. The form was later called rhyme royal. It is long enough to tell a bit of story and ends with a rhyming couplet that can sum up or turn it.

blocks.name: gb-rhyme-royal
blocks.cap: The first stanza, with its rhymes colored. Switch on "Word help" for glosses.

blocks.title: Counting stanzas
blocks.q: If a book of the poem has 1,092 lines, all in rhyme royal, how many stanzas is that?
steps: Each stanza has 7 lines.

blocks.name: gb-fortune-wheel
blocks.cap: Our own summary of each book. Fortune's wheel lifts Troilus to the top in Book III, then lets him fall.

blocks.html: The plot is simple; the poem is long because Chaucer lets us into his characters' minds. Troilus, who laughed at lovers, falls in love and is helpless. Pandarus is a talkative, clever friend and matchmaker, full of proverbs. Criseyde is thoughtful and cautious, a widow alone in a city at war, whose father, the prophet Calchas, has gone over to the Greeks. When the Trojans trade her to the Greek camp, she means to return; but she is frightened and alone, and in the end she accepts the Greek Diomede.

Chaucer, as narrator, refuses to condemn her harshly. He says he would excuse her if he could, for she was so sorry for what she did. Readers have argued ever since whether Criseyde is faithless, or a person caught by Fortune and fear.
In the opening of Book II, Chaucer asks his readers not to laugh at the old-fashioned ways of lovers in his story. Language and customs change, he says, and that is natural.

Chaucer's point is truer than he could know: his own English now needs glosses. Over about 650 years, the sounds of English vowels shifted (the "Great Vowel Shift"), many endings dropped away, and thousands of words changed meaning.

Chaucer translated Boethius's Consolation of Philosophy, a Roman book written in prison about Fortune, fate and God's knowledge, and its ideas run all through Troilus. In Book IV, Troilus, alone in a temple, argues at length that everything must happen as God foresees it, so he cannot be free. Boethius had answered that argument; Troilus, in his grief, does not hear the answer.

Thinking the poem simply blames Criseyde. Chaucer shows a world where people want to be faithful but are moved by fear, chance and pressure. He asks us to see how hard faithfulness is, and also how much it matters.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

After Troilus is killed in battle, his spirit rises to the eighth sphere of heaven. From there he looks down at the little Earth and laughs at the grief of those weeping for him, seeing how small earthly troubles are beside heaven. Chaucer then turns to his young readers, urging them to love God, who will never betray anyone who trusts him. He sends the poem off ("Go, little book") and asks his friends, the poet John Gower and the philosopher Ralph Strode, to correct it.
Readers argue about this ending. Does it reject the love story, crown it, or set it in a larger frame? The same view from the heavens appears in Dante's Paradiso, which Chaucer knew.

The Scottish poet Robert Henryson wrote a sequel, and Shakespeare's darker play Troilus and Cressida (later on this ladder) retold the story again. "Pandar," from Pandarus, even became an English word, though Chaucer's Pandarus is a warmer friend than the word suggests.

items: Is Criseyde to blame, or Fortune, or the war? Can it be all three?
Troilus thinks that if God knows the future, we are not free. How might Boethius or Aquinas answer him?
Why does Chaucer end a love story by looking down from the stars?
Chaucer says that ways of speaking change in a thousand years. What words of ours might sound strange in the year 3000?

blocks.html: Compare Homer's Iliad for the war, Dante for the heavens, and Shakespeare's Troilus and Cressida for a different telling.

💬 Talk about it together

  1. Have you ever made a promise that was very hard to keep? What made it hard?
  2. Pandarus is a helpful friend, but is he always a good one? What makes a good friend?
  3. Do you think Criseyde should be blamed? Why or why not?
  4. Fortune's wheel goes up and down. Is life really like that? What stays the same when the wheel turns?
  5. Read one Middle English line aloud together. Which words could you guess?

blocks.html: A note for parents: Some tales are bawdy, notably the Miller's, the Reeve's, the Merchant's and the Shipman's. This lesson only names them. The Knight's, Nun's Priest's, Franklin's and Pardoner's tales suit families.

Choose a path

  • 🌱 For young readers
  • 📖 For teens and adults
  • 🔭 Going deeper

🌱 For young readers

About ages 8 to 12. Read it together, or on your own.

Imagine a big group of travelers on horseback: a knight whose tunic is still stained with rust from his armor, a cook, a miller who plays the bagpipes, a nun with her little dogs, a student who loves books more than money, a sailor, a doctor, and a lady from the town of Bath who has been to Jerusalem three times. They are riding together from London to the city of Canterbury, to visit the tomb of a saint. To pass the time, they agree to tell stories.

That is The Canterbury Tales, by Geoffrey Chaucer, written a little over 600 years ago. The innkeeper, Harry Bailly, comes along as judge. Whoever tells the best story will win a free supper at his inn when they get back.

blocks.name: gb-pilgrim-route

blocks.html: One of the best-loved tales is told by a priest. It is about a proud rooster named Chauntecleer, who has a bad dream about a fox. His wife, the hen Pertelote, tells him dreams mean nothing. The next morning a sly fox flatters Chauntecleer into closing his eyes and singing, then grabs him by the neck and runs. But the clever rooster talks his way out, and both learn a lesson about flattery.

🧩 Try this

Your own pilgrimage. With your family, plan a pretend journey. Each person picks a character (a knight, a cook, a student, a sailor ...) and tells a short story that suits that character. Who should be the judge? What prize will the best story win?

For parents: some tales are rude or bawdy. Good ones to share: the Nun's Priest's Tale (the rooster and the fox), the Knight's Tale, the Franklin's Tale, and the Pardoner's Tale (a fable about greed in which three men come to a bad end).

📖 For teens and adults

The full lesson.

Geoffrey Chaucer (c. 1343–1400) worked for three kings of England as a soldier, diplomat and official, and wrote poems in his spare hours. He began The Canterbury Tales around 1387 and was still working on it when he died in 1400. He was buried in Westminster Abbey, the first poet in what became Poets' Corner.

The pilgrims are going to the shrine of Saint Thomas Becket in Canterbury Cathedral. Becket, archbishop of Canterbury, was killed in his cathedral in 1170 after a quarrel with King Henry II, and was soon made a saint. His shrine became the most famous pilgrimage site in England.

Read the last two lines aloud: seke ("seek") rhymes with seke ("sick"). Chaucer wrote mostly in rhymed pairs of ten-syllable lines, later called heroic couplets. In his English, a final -e was often sounded: A-pril-le, so-te.

Chaucer, as a pilgrim himself, meets "wel nyne and twenty" travelers at the Tabard Inn in Southwark and describes each one. Together they make a picture of English society: the knightly class (Knight, Squire), the church (Prioress, Monk, Friar, Parson, Pardoner, Summoner), and the working and middle ranks (Merchant, Lawyer, Doctor, Miller, Cook, Shipman, Plowman, the Wife of Bath and more).

Chaucer's portraits are sly. He seems to praise everyone, but the details tell the truth: the Monk loves hunting more than prayer, the Friar knows every innkeeper better than every poor man, and the Pardoner sells fake relics. A few, such as the poor Parson and his brother the Plowman, are shown as plainly good. The Clerk, a poor Oxford student, is one of them.

The Host proposes that each pilgrim tell two tales on the way and two on the way back; the best wins a supper paid for by the rest. They draw straws, and the Knight goes first. The plan was far too big. Chaucer finished about 24 tales, some of them incomplete, and the pilgrims never get back to the Tabard.

blocks.title: The Host's plan
blocks.q: If 30 pilgrims (29 plus Chaucer) each told four tales, how many tales would the book have had? About what fraction did Chaucer write?
steps: $30 \times 4 = 120$ tales planned.
About 24 survive: $24 \div 120 = \tfrac{1}{5}$.
blocks.a: 120 tales; Chaucer wrote about a fifth of the plan

The rooster Chauntecleer, his dream, and the flattering fox.
Three young men set out to kill Death and find a heap of gold instead; their greed destroys them. His theme, in Latin: Radix malorum est cupiditas, "greed is the root of evils."
A wife, a rash promise and a magician; each character tries to outdo the others in generosity.
His jingling "Sir Thopas" is so bad the Host stops him; he tells a long prose tale of wise counsel instead.

blocks.cap: Some of the tales, summarized in our own words. Others, such as the Miller's and the Reeve's, are rough comedies for adults.

blocks.html: The links between tales are as lively as the tales. Pilgrims interrupt, quarrel and answer each other. The Miller insists on going next; the Reeve, who was once a carpenter, takes offense; the Wife of Bath gives a long, funny speech about her five marriages and who should rule in a household.

Thinking the book mocks religion. Chaucer satirizes churchmen who betray their calling, which many writers of his time did, but he also gives the Parson, the most admired pilgrim, the last word, and ends the book with a short prayer asking forgiveness for his works.

🔭 Going deeper

Context, the big questions, and how later books answered.

Chaucer did not invent the idea of a frame story: Boccaccio's Decameron has ten young people telling a hundred tales. Chaucer's twist is that his tellers are a mix of every rank, and that the tales reveal the tellers. The story each pilgrim chooses, and the way they tell it, is part of their portrait.

Chaucer wrote in the English of London when French and Latin were still the languages of the court and of learning. The success of his poems helped make London English the basis of written English. William Caxton printed the Tales around 1476, one of the first books printed in England.

The Tales survive in more than 80 manuscripts, in groups called "fragments" whose order is uncertain. Scholars still debate the order Chaucer intended and whether the closing Retraction was meant as an ending.

items: Does a story tell you more about the person who tells it, or about the world?
Chaucer praises good people and mocks hypocrites. Is satire a good way to make people better?
What would a "General Prologue" of your own town or school include?
Why do you think travelers tell stories?

blocks.html: Compare Dante's Comedy, another journey with a guide and a goal, and Boccaccio's Decameron. Later on this ladder, Shakespeare inherits Chaucer's English and his gallery of characters.

💬 Talk about it together

  1. Which pilgrim would you most like to ride beside? Which would you avoid?
  2. The Host offers a prize for the best story. What makes a story "best": being funny, being true, or teaching something?
  3. In the Nun's Priest's Tale, the fox flatters the rooster and the rooster flatters the fox. How can you tell flattery from real praise?
  4. The Clerk would "gladly lerne, and gladly teche." Who in your life is like that?
  5. Read the first two lines aloud together. What do you hear that sounds like English today?
